en: The Ritual for Repentance and Vows for Rebirth in the Pure Land,
compiled by the Śramaṇa Zunshi: Having excerpted from the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* in its extensive version, as well as various Mahāyāna sūtras such as the *Praise of the Pure Land*,
I have assembled these methods to circulate among future generations, so that all may universally form pure karmic conditions.
Tracing the origin of this, the Buddhas, out of compassion for sentient beings who are lost and blind,
have established many skillful means to guide and draw them in. Yet,
which among these provides the most peaceful sustenance and pure karma that can be cultivated with direct and swift efficacy?
All Mahāyāna sūtras initiate this essential point;
there are none among the Buddhas of the ten directions who do not praise it.
Whether they be bhikṣus, the fourfold assembly, or virtuous men and women, [they should all uphold it].
Those with either impaired or complete faculties who wish to swiftly shatter the various darknesses of ignorance,
and who wish to eternally extinguish the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds.
For those who have committed grave offenses that violate the prohibitions, as well as other minor transgressions,
they should practice this method if they wish to restore their purity once again.
When the various precepts, both great and small, are manifested before them,
they attain the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*) and are able to fulfill all the bodhisattva gates of the pāramitās.
One should train in this Dharma if one desires to be free from all fears at the time of death,
and to experience physical and mental peace, well-being, and joy as if returning home.
The light illuminates their dwelling,
and extraordinary fragrances and music arise;
Amitābha Buddha, Avalokiteśvara, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta appear before them.
They are escorted to the Purple Gold Terrace and received by the outstretched hand of the Buddha.
Transversely cutting across the five paths of rebirth, they gallop through the nine grades of existence;
casting off the afflictions of heat and distress, they find rest in cool serenity.
Those who, upon first leaving behind worldly afflictions,
immediately reach the stage of non-retrogression and attain the realization of non-arising without passing through long eons,
should study this Dharma.
Desiring to cultivate even a small dharma and thereby evoke a wondrous retribution,
the Buddhas of the ten directions simultaneously extol them and bestow predictions of enlightenment before their very eyes.
Having made offerings to incalculable Buddhas in a single thought-moment, they immediately return to their own lands.
Sitting and eating together with Amitābha,
engaging in discourse with Avalokiteśvara,
and walking with Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
The eyes and ears see through and hear across;
the body’s dimensions are boundless as it flies through space;
and with mastery over past lives, one possesses perfect clarity.
He perceives the five realms of existence as reflections in a mirror,
and in every thought-moment he realizes and enters the inexhaustible samādhi;
such descriptions are beyond measure.
One should practice this sublime Dharma;
all that has been spoken is true and not false.
The Buddhas of the ten directions extend their broad and long tongues.
He praised this matter to demonstrate its non-falsity.
How could we, his disciples, dare not believe the Buddha?
We now take the various sutras on the Pure Land as the basis for establishing these ritual practices.
If you wish to know this in detail, consult the sutras for further benefit;
for now, I shall briefly explain it in ten sections.
First: Adorning and Purifying the Site of Practice (Dharmapada).
Second, explaining the method of skillful means;
third, clarifying the intent of correct cultivation;
fourth, burning incense and scattering flowers.
Five: The method for requesting [teachings].
Six: The method for praising.
Seven: The method for paying homage to the Buddha and the Dharma.
8. The method of repentance and aspiration;
9. The method of circumambulatory recitation;
10. The method of seated meditation.
1. Purifying the Site of Practice (Dharmaparyāya-maṇḍala): First, one should select a secluded and quiet chamber for the site of practice.
First, remove the old soil;
afterwards, take fresh soil from a quiet location.
The ground must be cleared of tiles and stones,
and previously unpolluted materials shall be used to fill it; then,
smear it with fragrant substances to make it utterly pure.
Next, suspend a new precious canopy above it;
from within the canopy, hang five variegated banners,
and throughout the chamber, hang various silk streamers, banners, and flowers.
Select fine ornaments and install the Buddha image seated facing east in the western position,
with Avalokiteśvara attending on the left.
Śrīkṣetra (Avalokiteśvara) stands as an attendant to the right.
In front of the image, various excellent flowers and lotuses should be placed;
it is best to install nine images of those reborn in the Pure Land.
It is also not a hindrance if they are absent.
As for the remaining items for the ritual adornment, arrange them according to one's capacity.
Next, provide mats and seats all around, taking care that the ground is not damp.
The practitioner must wear fresh and clean robes;
if no fresh and clean ones are available at all, they should wash and dye the finest garment from among those already owned.
Only after bathing and putting these on should they enter the ritual arena (*maṇḍala*).
One should enter and exit through the left and right sides of the doorway.
Shoes and sandals must be kept neat and orderly, not in disarray.
When departing for one's destination, one must change into old clothes.
After bathing, one puts on clean robes;
this is done daily in this manner.
Next, at the site of practice (maṇḍala),...
One should personally exhaust all resources to make various offerings to the Triple Gem.
If one does not offer everything one possesses,
the practice of the Dharma will lack single-minded devotion, and there will certainly be no response or descent of blessings.
Just as one must first exhaust all that belongs to oneself before seeking externally, so too for practitioners:
ten people is the limit;
more than that is not permissible.
It is appropriate to begin on one of the six fast days (ṣaḍ-upoṣadha). 2.

Clarifying the Method of Skillful Means (Upāya-dharma-vyakti): Second, regarding the clarification of the method of skillful means, if a practitioner wishes to enter the maṇḍala but their body and mind are distracted, [they should proceed as follows].
One must prepare in advance by arranging a separate room for seven days;
it must not be in the same location as the site of practice.
Just as it is permitted to share a room even when there is no separate building,
one should practice and test oneself day and night,
and also pre-recite the texts for the five repentances and so forth.
He became so thoroughly proficient that he mastered dyeing,
washing, sewing, and all intermediate tasks;
all other miscellaneous affairs of livelihood were immediately brought to a halt.
Simply maintain the thought that before long you will certainly be born in the Pure Land.
Seek repentance with single-minded devotion so that no obstacles arise.
Each person should set a specific deadline and disregard their own body and life.
One must resolutely undertake pure karma so that it is immediately accomplished.
One must not allow even a single thought to dwell upon the five sensory objects.
One should censure and cast away craving and desire, and diligently subdue anger and delusion.
Practitioners each possess beginningless evil habits;
they should quickly seek to abandon them rather than merely performing formal repentance.
One should naturally observe the hindrances;
determine which habitual tendencies are predominant,
and then apply the appropriate method of rejection or balanced cultivation.
Take it up and restore it to its original state;
do not allow the practice of the dharma to result in wasted effort.
This can be understood through the power of intention.
3. Clarifying the Intent of Correct Cultivation, Part Three. Regarding the clarification of the intent of correct cultivation: the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* clarifies a period of seven times seven days;
the *Duṅ-yin-wang* (Dundubhisvara-rāja) and the *Mahā-amitābha-sūtra* clarify ten days and ten nights.
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* (Sixteen Contemplations Sutra) and the *Amitābha-sūtra* clarify that one should take seven days and seven nights as the period;
these three [texts] together establish this as the duration.
It must by no means be reduced.
Regarding the meaning of "correct cultivation," Vasubandhu’s treatise states:
What is the meaning of "clarifying"? It means contemplating the Land of Peace and Bliss and beholding Amitābha Buddha, with the aspiration to be born in that land.
How does one contemplate?
How does one give rise to faith?
Those who practice the five gates of mindfulness and achieve them will ultimately attain birth in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
One beholds Amitābha Buddha. What are the five?
First is the gate of prostration.
Second is the gate of praise;
third is the gate of making vows;
fourth is the gate of contemplation.
Fifth is the gate of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
Regarding the bodhisattva’s skillful means of dedication,
this refers to the teaching of the five types of practice, beginning with prostration.
Regarding all the roots of merit and virtue thus accumulated,
they do not seek the happiness of maintaining their own person,
but desire to uproot the suffering of all sentient beings.
To form a vow to embrace all sentient beings so that they may together be born in that Land of Peace and Bliss of the Buddha is called the Bodhisattva’s skillful means of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
Thus, by skillfully knowing dedication,
one attains three gateways that accord with enlightenment:
first, an unstained and pure mind.
First, because one does not seek various pleasures for oneself;
second, the mind of peaceful purity,
because one uproots the suffering of all sentient beings.
Third is the pure mind of joy,
which causes all sentient beings to attain great bodhi,
because it gathers in sentient beings so that they may be born in that land.
Therefore, the entire treatise is employed here as the primary intent;
the addition of the practice of repentance is solely for the purpose of eliminating obstacles to rebirth.
In order to follow the Buddha’s compassion and swiftly deliver sentient beings,
one must with single-minded devotion and focused intent practice for seven times seven days,
or at least for seven days and nights during the six periods of the day and night.
Pay homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions and to the World-Honored One Amitābha.
Whether sitting or walking, do not allow your mind to be distracted.
Do not entertain thoughts of the five worldly desires for even as long as it takes to snap one's fingers.
Even when engaging with outsiders in conversation or jesting,
one must not use pretexts to delay, nor succumb to negligence or sleep;
rather, one should maintain uninterrupted mindfulness throughout every moment of rising and sitting.
To seek rebirth, one must practice with single-minded diligence.
Question: Since the methods of practice are so numerous, what does "single-minded" mean?
Answer: There is both principle and phenomenon.
First is the single mind of principle, which refers to when one first enters the ritual arena (maṇḍala).
Even though one may ultimately engage in manifold activities,
they are all devoid of intrinsic nature, neither arising nor ceasing;
they share the single characteristic of the dharma-realm, in accordance with the conditions of the dharma-realm.
The first is the single-mindedness of principle;
the second is the single-mindedness of phenomena.
This refers, for example, when one is prostrating to the Buddha.
Do not think of other matters;
simply devote yourself exclusively to prostrating before the Buddha.
Reciting the sutras and practicing the Way should likewise be done in this manner.
This is called single-mindedness regarding the ritual object. 4.
Burning Incense and Scattering Flowers: Fourth, when the practitioner who has already purified the three karmas first enters the *maṇḍala*, they should burn incense and scatter flowers.
First, one should correctly establish this reflection:
"For the sake of sentient beings,
I have resolved to attain bodhicitta."
In order to seek rebirth in the Pure Land,
one should pay universal homage to the Triple Gem and extensively cultivate offerings.
When the Triple Gem receives offerings,
they will surely think of me and act according to my requests.
Bear witness to my vow.
This burning of incense and scattering of flowers is also called the offering of the three karmas.
First, pay general homage to the Triple Gem.
There is no need to visualize each one individually according to their respective directions;
simply visualize yourself and all the Buddhas of the ten directions.
The essence of the reality of true marks is fundamentally devoid of subject and object;
therefore, there is neither one who worships nor one who is worshipped.
This absence of subject and object is termed the ocean of the dharma-realm.
May all sentient beings likewise perceive this principle;
this is called "entering together.
First, one should chant: "With all reverence and single-minded devotion, we pay homage to the Buddhas who eternally abide throughout the ten directions and the Dharma-realm."
With single-minded devotion, pay homage to the eternally abiding Dharma throughout the ten directions and the entire dharma-realm.
With single-minded devotion, pay homage to the eternally abiding Sangha throughout the ten directions and the entire dharma-realm. Having chanted these words, each person takes up an incense burner.
Kneeling again, they said:
"All these members of the assembly shall each kneel and reverently hold incense and flowers to make offerings according to the Dharma."
Having completed the offerings to the Triple Gem throughout the ten directions and the entire dharma-realm, the chanting is suspended here.
Each person releases their incense burner and holds loose flowers in their hands.
Extensively perform the offerings,
visualizing that these incense and flowers pervade the ten directions,
forming a subtle and wondrous platform of light.
The celestial music and divine precious incense;
the celestial delicacies and divine precious garments;
the inconceivable, wondrous dust of the Dharma.
From each and every atom emerge all atoms;
from each and every atom emerge all dharmas.
They revolve without obstruction, mutually adorning one another.
Reaching everywhere before the Triple Gem in the ten directions,
and before the Triple Gem throughout the Dharma-realm of the ten directions—
in all these places, my body performs offerings.
Each and every one pervades the entire Dharma-realm;
they are mutually distinct yet without obstruction,
performing the work of Buddhas throughout the limits of the future.
Universally perfuming all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm,
may those who receive this perfume all give rise to the Bodhicitta;
together entering the state of non-arising, they shall realize the Buddha-wisdom.
Having formed this visualization, scatter flowers,
take up an incense burner, and utter these words:
"May these clouds of incense and flowers..."
Pervading the realms of the ten directions,
they make offerings to all Buddhas,
the Honored Dharma, and all Bodhisattvas.
An immeasurable assembly of śrāvakas,
having raised a platform of radiance,
transcended boundless realms.
Within boundless Buddha-fields,
they perform the work of Buddhas,
universally perfuming all sentient beings.
All generate the bodhicitta. [The following line] "All generate" is joined with the next phrase, "And make offerings," which is sung solo.
Having finished the offerings, everyone rises with reverence and performs one prostration.
5. The Fifth Method: The Ritual of Invocation. Regarding the ritual of invocation, one should again add incense as before, kneeling with the right knee on the ground.
Holding the incense burner, maintain a focused mind and act with diligent reverence, universally inviting the Triple Gem to enter the dharma-assembly.
One must not hastily invite the Most Honored One;
rather, one should offer the invitation with the three karmas applied with urgency and the single-minded devotion.
If it is not done in this way, the invitation will be in vain and of no benefit.
Visualize each Tathāgata, according to their respective directions,
leading their retinues into my place of practice,
appearing as if dwelling right before one's eyes and filling the entirety of space.
One must not allow a single moment of distracted thought to arise; however,
the invitation is performed only on the eighth day,
and is not required at other times.
The leader chants: "With one mind, we reverently invite:
Namo to our Original Teacher Śākyamuni Buddha. Śākyamuni is our teacher;
he expounded the various Mahāyāna teachings, enabling us to cultivate the practices for the Pure Land."
Therefore, one must first make the request.
Each should direct their mind to feel gratitude for this benevolent virtue.
Thus, the request is made three times.
At each invocation, one should contemplate, saying:
"The nature of my three karmas is like empty space;
Śākyamuni Tathāgata is likewise."
The Unarisen Ultimate Reality acts for the sake of sentient beings;
together with the assembly, it comes to receive offerings.
The following provides a general model for the three requests.
With single-minded devotion, we take refuge in and entreat the fifty-three Buddhas of the past, from immeasurable kalpas ago:
Dīpaṃkara Buddha, Prabhūtaratna Buddha, Nāgarāja Buddha, and so forth. These fifty-three Buddhas appeared before the Bhikṣu Dharmākara had yet entered the world.
In this sequence, there have been these fifty-four Buddhas;
it was only during the time of the Buddha Lokeśvararāja that [the Bodhisattva] requested [the vows] from the Teacher Dharmākara—
this should be understood as being the same as the previous verses on visualization.
Simply change the name of the Buddha and invoke him with single-minded devotion:
"Namo to the World-Sovereign King Buddha of the Past, Long Extinct; World-King Buddha, who is the original teacher of Dharmākara."
One must know that when making requests, they should be made in reliance upon the forty-eight vows originally made by that Buddha.
The verses are the same as before.
The text is revised to state: "The Buddha Sovereign King (Vaiśravaṇarāja) is also like this.
This Buddha, together with the previous fifty-three Buddhas, appears in the *Mahā-amitāyur-dhyāna-sūtra*.
With single-minded devotion,
we take refuge in the Buddhas of the present throughout the ten directions, such as Akṣobhya Buddha,
and in all the Buddhas of the pure lands as numerous as the sands of the rivers throughout the ten directions— these Buddhas of the ten directions.
All of them extend their broad and long tongues,
covering the entire trichiliocosm to praise the Land of Ultimate Bliss; therefore,
one must request that they protect and mindfully remember [the practitioner].
When reciting the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*,
one should visualize that [the Buddhas] come from those ten directions at the time of invitation.
The verse is revised as follows:
"The Buddhas of the ten directions are likewise so.
All else remains the same as before.
With single-minded devotion,
we take refuge in the Seven Buddhas of the Past and the Thousand Buddhas of the Future Auspicious Aeon.
I single-mindedly entreat all Buddhas of the three periods of time:
Homage to Amitābha Buddha of the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Amitābha is the Lord of Repentance and Vows.
One should imagine that they lead their boundless retinues to my place of practice (bodhimaṇḍa), where they receive my acceptance and protective mindfulness;
each sheds tears and earnestly makes their request three times.
One must certainly come and sit upright at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
All other Buddhas and Bodhisattvas shall serve as witnesses.
Change the verse as before.
Regarding this final request,
one should know that it accords with the *Samantabhadra Repentance Method*.
With single-minded devotion, make this invocation.
Homage to the Mahāyāna Sutra of the Forty-eight Vows of Amitāyus,
the Sutra of Praise,
and all other sutras and teachings pertaining to that Pure Land.
One should contemplate the true and pure Dharma-treasure of all the honored sutras throughout the ten directions as being twofold: first, the Dharma-treasure of the ten directions;
second, the Dharma-treasure of the twelve divisions [of scripture].
Second is the Dharma-treasure of the Pure Land.
When visualizing the Dharma of the Pure Land,
one should visualize everywhere that the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, water birds, and musical trees all proclaim the sublime Dharma.
Manifest at the site of practice (maṇḍala) in accordance with my invitation,
so that my maṇḍala may be no different from that Pure Land.
Contemplate thus:
The nature of phenomena is like space, beyond all perception;
the Dharma Jewel in these two realms is inconceivable.
I now entreat you with my three karmas in accordance with the Dharma.
Appearing simultaneously, they receive the offerings.
With a single mind, we reverently invite:
Namo Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva.
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva,
Ajita Bodhisattva, Anikṣiptadhura Bodhisattva, and others.
All the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas join in requesting the Buddha with verses;
however, one should simply change the wording to say, "The great Bodhisattvas do likewise.
At the time of making this request, one should visualize Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and all others as being present in the Pure Land.
As stated in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*, one should single-mindedly offer this invocation:
"Namo to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara of the World of Ultimate Bliss. One should visualize this Bodhisattva seated upon a lotus throne, attending to the left side of the Buddha.
Their majestic power and radiant light are all immeasurable.
Recite the verses as before.
With single-minded devotion, offer this invocation.

Homage to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta of the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Visualize this Bodhisattva seated upon a lotus throne, attending to the Buddha at his right side, no different from Avalokiteśvara.
With single-minded devotion,
we take refuge in and entreat the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Dharmākara Bhikṣu of incalculable kalpas past— the very body that served as the cause for Amitābha—
who cultivated forty-eight vows to gather in and transform all sentient beings.
One should contemplate this debt of gratitude.
The verses are as previously stated.
With single-minded devotion, one should offer this invocation.

Homage to the great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas of the Land of Ultimate Bliss who have newly resolved their minds on the Path, those of non-arising and non-retrogression, and those in their final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*). As the sutra states: "The great Bodhisattvas of non-retrogression and those in their final birth."
When making the request, one should form this mental visualization.
The verse is as before.
Request with single-minded devotion.
Homage to Śāriputra and all others of this land.
With the thought that all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and noble saṅghas who have attained the Way pervade the entire dharma-realm, I universally invite these noble saṅghas;
with single-minded devotion, I respectfully invite them.
In this land, there are the Brahmā, Śakra, and the Four Great Kings,
along with all the hosts of devas, the Lord of Māras,
and the various kings of nāgas and ghosts.

Yama, the Lord of the Five Realms who punishes evil and protects the True Dharma, and the Guardian Spirit of the Monastery—may all such worthy sages likewise be invited three times to come here to provide protection;
one should know that this applies to all except for those for whom prostration is required.
I respectfully invite the World-Honored One Amitābha,
Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara,
and Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
Pure Ocean Assembly, all worthy and holy ones:
I pray that you will not forsake your great kindness and great compassion;
with the unimpeded vision and hearing of the path of the other-mind knowledge and the mastery of the supernormal power of the body.
Descending to the site of enlightenment, you abide upon the Dharma-seat;
may your light shine everywhere to gather us in,
and out of compassion, protect and shelter us so that we may achieve the vows and practices for Bodhi.
Śākyamuni Buddha, Dīpaṃkara Buddha,
and Lokêśvararāja Buddha.
All the Perfectly Awakened Ones of the ten directions and three periods of time,
as well as the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī and the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.
May the noble assemblies of the Three Vehicles,
out of their great compassion, all come to protect and sustain us;
as well as the hosts of devas, māras, brahmās, nāgas, and ghosts.

May all the deities who protect the Dharma and all worthy sages arrive at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), offering consolation and steadfastly maintaining their commitment to collectively accomplish pure conduct. (Recite this three times. 6.
The Sixth Section: Praising the Dharma. One should rise, pay respectful homage, and join one’s palms.
Your complexion is like Jambu-river gold; your face surpasses the pure full moon.
The radiance of your body and wisdom is brilliant, illuminating without limit, subduing hosts of Māras and enemies, and skillfully transforming all humans and devas.
Riding upon that vessel of the Eightfold Noble Path, you are able to ferry across those who find it difficult to cross;
by merely hearing your name, one attains non-retrogression. Therefore, I take refuge and pay homage to you, extolling your buddha-qualities in this way.
They cultivate the unsurpassed roots of goodness of the Mahāyāna and offer their merit to the devas,
nāgas, and the eight classes of supernatural beings in the higher realms, to the Great Brahmā King and the Heaven of the Thirty-three,
and to Yama, the five paths of rebirth, the six fast days, and the eight kings.
The various kings of pestilence spirits, each with their retinues;
the local deities of this land who protect the True Dharma within the monasteries;
and furthermore, for the kings, sovereigns, and the myriad people of the realm.
To one's preceptors and parents, virtuous and non-virtuous spiritual friends,
temple patrons, and the faithful offerings from the ten directions;
extending widely to all sentient beings throughout the Dharma realm.
May I, by means of these roots of goodness, cultivate them with equanimity;
through the two kinds of adornment— merit and wisdom—
may I be born together in the Land of Bliss at the time of death.
7. Chapter Seven: Paying Homage to the Buddha-Dharma. Having finished praising the Buddha-Dharma, one should pay homage to all Buddhas.
When paying homage to the Buddhas:
One should contemplate that all Buddhas are one’s compassionate fathers, for they enable one to be born in the pure lands of the Buddhas; thus, with single-minded reverence, one pays homage.
When the Master Śākyamuni has finished chanting, one performs a prostration.
Contemplation on the Clouds:
The nature of both the one who prostrates and the object of prostration is empty and quiescent;
the mutual resonance of cause and response is inconceivable.
This my place of enlightenment is like a sovereign jewel;
within it, the shadow of Śākyamuni Tathāgata appears,
and my own shadow appears before Śākyamuni.
Placing one's head at the feet in direct encounter, one takes refuge and pays homage.
The following sections shall use this same formula.
With single-minded reverence, one pays homage.
In the distant past, during kalpas long ago,
there were fifty-three Buddhas, such as Dīpaṃkara Buddha, Prabhūtaratna Buddha, and Nāgarāja Buddha, as described in the ritual invocation.
One should contemplate this body as being like an illusion or a magical transformation.
Visualizing oneself before that Buddha, one performs prostrations;
the verses are as above.
Simply change it to read: "Within the manifestation of the fifty-three Buddhas, my own body and shadow appear before all the Buddhas.
Below, follow this pattern accordingly.
With single-minded reverence, I pay homage to the World-Honored King of Dharma, who passed away long ago; to the Dharma-treasury; and to the Original Teacher, He Who Should Be Known.
With single-minded reverence, I pay homage.
The Buddhas of the east, such as Akṣobhya,
and all the Buddhas of the pure lands throughout the sands of the Ganges in the eastern direction— all the Buddhas of the ten directions below this point— extend their broad and long tongues.
Praise the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
One should imagine this body before the Buddhas of pure lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River,
and with single-minded devotion, pay respectful homage.
I pay single-minded homage to the Buddha Supreme and Vast Cloud-Thunder Sound King of the Southeastern Quarter,
and to all the Buddhas of every pure land as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the southeastern direction.
I pay single-minded homage to the Buddhas of the South, such as the Buddha Sun-Moon Radiance,
and to all the Buddhas of the pure lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the southern direction.
To the Buddha named Supreme Sunlight Renown and Merit in the southwest,
and to all the Buddhas of the pure lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the entire southwest,
I pay homage with a single mind.

I pay homage with a single mind to all the Buddhas of the pure lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the northern direction, beginning with the Buddha Immeasurable Light-Adorned Penetrating Enlightenment Wisdom.
I pay single-minded homage to the countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Buddhas,
such as Vipula-mati, and to all the Buddhas of the pure lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the northeast.

In the direction below, there are the Buddhas such as Sarvadharmanayadharmaprabhāsaśrītejorāja, who constantly radiate the light of supreme virtue,
as well as all the Buddhas of the pure lands, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, in the direction below.
With single-minded reverence,

Postscript to the Ritual for Repentance and Vows for Rebirth in the Pure Land: This dharma was compiled by me.
It has now been revised twice.
The previous edition was already carved into woodblocks and widely circulated by the monk Chiekyō of Echigo.
The opening of its postscript states:
"I, having unworthily partaken of the ancestral teachings," and so forth.
Since the ranks of the sages are thus vast, [the lineage is extensive].
Recently, I have observed that the practice of bowing and rising causes excessive fatigue;
therefore, the methods of repentance and meditation shall all involve the elimination of such formalities,
while everything else shall remain as it was in the past.
The current expanded and abbreviated versions are already sufficiently reliable for transmission and practice;
let future worthies not be confused by their differences.
May they be carefully edited, annotated, and supplemented.
What need is there to lament its exquisite composition?
